I read a comment that "teachers are overpaid", and it got me thinking. So I'm pitching my idea here. Keep in mind, I'm not an American, so things may be different for you yanks as opposed to us skippies.

Are teachers overpaid? Yes and no.

To answer this question, one must consider who is ultimately paying: the parents. I'm not sure about the US, but there are definitely schools where places are only open to students that live in the area. And in these areas, the price of housing is much greater than similar surrounding areas. This implies that a good education is worth up to hundreds or thousands of dollars to some people. In this context, 1-2k per year extra in school fees/teacher wages is a relatively small amount, yet constitutes between 30-60k extra per class (teacher) per year. Another way to consider their price is looking at the cost of a tutor, which is around $50/hour for a professional, and even as high as $35/hour for a good college student. Though this is a bit rough an indicator, as tutoring is usually an hour or two a week, not the full 40.

At the same time, there are teachers who are downright rubbish, and should be paid less because they're either not as good, or downright destructive (brainwashing kids with Marxism).

Bad teacher, or shitty student?

This is yet another complication to consider. Some teachers are very good in that they can teach, know their material back to front and can engage the students such they can construct their own conclusions, but they cannot control a class for shit. Conversely, you have teachers that can instill discipline, and make even the most disruptive of students sit quietly at their desk and study; but their understanding of the content is barely above that of the rest of the class. Obviously, every teacher wants to teach the smart, quiet students who will do well regardless of how they teach, are lower stress and reflect well on them as a teacher.

My proposed solution is as follows

You grab all the students in a 'pool' with their average grades, and record available, and have a 'bidding' process between eligible teachers, starting at zero dollars. The amount bid, is the amount per/hour that a teacher is willing to teach that student for, and will be paid for by the parents. Unruly students will demand a higher price, being difficult to teach. However all this does consider the student, without considering the teacher, so the parents must also have some input.

The second part is to then present the bids of each teacher (and relevant "stats"), to the parents. The parents can then consider each teacher per subject: their years teaching, class averages, average improvement of students in their class, etc. And decide whose offers they will accept. In this way, parents of not-so-good students can still get their kid a good teacher, but they'll be paying a premium for it. They can also get a teacher with more experience, and in this way, better teachers can still make more money than other teachers because they're relying on dedicated parents willing to pay more for their student to have a better teacher.

The students will finally be sorted into class based first on student preference of the highest price they're willing to pay, and secondly by the lowest price the teachers are willing to accept. And the difference in teachers' pay rate will be determined by the sum of each of the students in their class. I say 'difference' because there are other school costs besides wages themselves that need to be paid for also.

Problems

As I was writing this, yet another factor came to mind: parents would be willing to pay more to NOT have a student in their class, or pay extra TO have a student in their class.
